1.title: Scalable and Loosely Coupled Architectures
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Scalable and Loosely Coupled Architectures. This module covers task statement two point one, the first task of Domain two, Design Resilient Architectures, which carries twenty-six percent of the exam. You will learn how to decouple components with queues, topics and events, scale each tier on its own, and choose between containers and serverless. The exam describes a growth problem and asks you to pick the service that fixes it.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Design event-driven, microservice and multi-tier architectures. Choose scaling strategies: horizontal or vertical, stateless or stateful. Pick the services for loose coupling: S Q S, S N S, EventBridge, Amazon M Q and Step Functions. Decide when to use containers and when to use serverless. And choose load balancers, caches, read replicas and A P I Gateway.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lantern and Loom Meets the Holiday Rush
1.text: A holiday sale is coming to Lantern and Loom, and traffic will grow tenfold. Today, checkout waits for the email service, so one slow call stalls the page. Customer sessions vanish whenever a web server is replaced. And partners want order events pushed to them. Your job is to make each part scale and fail on its own.

1.title: Tight and Loose Coupling
1.text: Start with the core idea. In a tightly coupled design, components call each other directly and wait. One slow or failed part stalls the rest, and everything scales together. In a loosely coupled design, components talk through an intermediary, so each part fails and recovers on its own, and scales independently. The intermediaries are queues, which is S Q S; topics, which is S N S; event buses, which is EventBridge; load balancers; A P I s; and workflows, which is Step Functions. They absorb spikes, retry, and let you deploy separately. Exam tip: spikes, retries or independent scaling mean put a queue, topic or event bus between the components.

1.title: Stateless and Stateful Workloads
1.text: A stateless server keeps no session data between requests, so any instance can serve any request. A stateful server keeps state on the instance, so requests must return to the same server, and a failure loses that state. The fix is to move state out: sessions to ElastiCache or DynamoDB, files to S three or E F S, and data to databases. Sticky sessions pin a client to one target, but they are a workaround, not the best design. Lambda is built for short tasks that keep no state between invocations. Exam tip: to scale out or replace servers freely, make the tier stateless and store state elsewhere.

1.title: Scaling Up and Scaling Out
1.text: There are two ways to scale. Vertical scaling, or scaling up, means a bigger instance. It has a ceiling, often needs a restart, and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, means more instances. It needs a stateless design and a load balancer, and it is highly resilient, because you can lose one and keep serving. For the web and application tiers, use Auto Scaling behind a load balancer, or containers that scale tasks. Scale queue workers on queue depth. For the data tier, use read replicas, caches and DynamoDB capacity. Exam tip: resilient and elastic usually means scale out, which means stateless.

1.title: Multi-Tier Architectures
1.text: A multi-tier architecture separates the web, application and data tiers. Everything except the load balancer sits in private subnets. A load balancer fronts each tier that needs one, and each tier scales on its own, across two or more Availability Zones. A cache shields the database, and a queue buffers background work. The figure shows the load balancer, the web and application tiers, the cache and database, and a queue feeding workers. Exam tip: separate the tiers so each can scale, fail and be replaced independently.

1.title: Choosing a Load Balancer
1.text: Elastic Load Balancing has four types. The Application Load Balancer, or A L B, works at layer seven for H T T P and H T T P S. It suits web apps, microservices and containers, with path and host routing and Lambda targets. The Network Load Balancer, or N L B, works at layer four for T C P, U D P and T L S. It handles millions of requests per second with low latency, and gives a static I P address per Availability Zone. The Gateway Load Balancer fronts third-party virtual appliances, such as firewalls. The Classic Load Balancer is the previous generation, so migrate away from it. All of them spread traffic across zones and run health checks. Exam tip: H T T P routing is A L B; static I P s or extreme performance is N L B.

1.title: Application Load Balancer Routing
1.text: An Application Load Balancer has listeners. A listener checks rules in priority order, and each rule has conditions and actions. You can route by path, host, header, method, query string or source I P address. A target group holds instances, I P addresses or Lambda functions, and has its own health checks. The load balancer can also redirect, return fixed responses, authenticate users, work with A W S W A F, and use A C M certificates. The figure shows one listener sending path-based requests to an A P I group, an images group and a default web group. Exam tip: many services behind one U R L, routed by path or host, means one A L B with several target groups.

1.title: Caching Strategies
1.text: Caching speeds up reads and takes load off the backend. At the edge, CloudFront, a C D N, caches content near users; module nine covers it. A P I Gateway can cache the responses of an A P I stage. ElastiCache caches query results and sessions. And Dax caches DynamoDB reads. Two strategies matter. Lazy loading loads data into the cache on a miss, caches only what is read, but can go stale. Write-through updates the cache on every write, so it is never stale, at the cost of extra writes. Add a T T L, short for time to live, to limit stale data and wasted space. Exam tip: fresh data on every read is write-through; cache only what is read is lazy loading.

1.title: Read Replicas and Data-Tier Scaling
1.text: An R D S read replica is a read-only copy, fed by asynchronous replication, that offloads reads. Replicas can sit in another Region, and can be promoted to a standalone database for disaster recovery. Replica data can lag, so reads may be slightly stale. R D S does not autoscale replicas; you add them. A Multi-A Z standby is different: replication is synchronous, and it cannot serve reads, because it exists for availability. For read-heavy workloads, pair replicas with a cache. Exam tip: to scale reads, use read replicas or a cache; to survive a failure, use Multi-A Z.

2.title: Amazon SQS Queues
2.text: Amazon S Q S is a hosted queue that decouples producers from consumers and buffers spikes. Standard queues use at-least-once delivery, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. Fifo queues provide exactly-once processing and ordering, with a high-throughput mode. The visibility timeout hides a message while it is processed, and the consumer deletes it when done. A dead-letter queue collects messages that keep failing. Retention runs from sixty seconds to fourteen days. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, a message holds up to one mebibyte, while older material says two hundred fifty-six kibibytes. Exam tip: to buffer work and scale consumers on queue depth, use S Q S; for strict order, use Fifo.

2.title: Amazon SNS Publish and Subscribe
2.text: Amazon S N S is publish and subscribe. A publisher sends to a topic, and S N S pushes a copy to every subscriber. Subscribers can be S Q S queues, Lambda functions, H T T P endpoints, email, S M S, mobile push, or Firehose. It supports application-to-application and application-to-person messages. Message filtering sends each subscriber only what it needs. There are standard and Fifo topics. S N S does not store messages for offline subscribers, so pair it with S Q S. Exam tip: one message to many consumers is S N S; add S Q S queues for durability.

2.title: Fan-Out with SNS and SQS
2.text: The fan-out pattern combines the two. The order service publishes once to an S N S topic. Each subscribed S Q S queue gets a copy, and its consumers process it at their own pace. A slow or failed consumer does not affect the others, and you can add a subscriber without changing the publisher. The figure shows one order message copied to queues for inventory, email and analytics, each with its own workers and dead-letter queue. Exam tip: fan-out with S N S plus S Q S gives one event, many independent, durable consumers.

2.title: Amazon EventBridge
2.text: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus. It connects A W S services, your own applications and software-as-a-service partners. Rules match event patterns and send events to targets, with optional transformation. Pipes give point-to-point connections from one source to one target, with filtering and enrichment. Scheduler runs cron, rate and one-time schedules. It is built for event-driven architectures, where producers do not know the consumers. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, the documentation describes a newer Custom Event Bus and the Classic one, so check which applies. Exam tip: routing events by content from many sources, or running schedules, is EventBridge.

2.title: Amazon MQ
2.text: Amazon M Q is a managed message broker for Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ. It supports J M S, A M Q P, M Q T T, Open Wire and Stomp. Its main use is to migrate an existing broker without rewriting the messaging code. Messages are encrypted at rest and in transit, and A W S handles setup, maintenance and upgrades. Multi-A Z designs keep brokers available. For new cloud-native applications, S Q S and S N S are simpler and scale further. Exam tip: an existing application that speaks J M S or A M Q P points to Amazon M Q.

2.title: Choosing a Messaging Service
2.text: Choosing a messaging service is about the verb. To buffer work, retry and absorb spikes, use S Q S. For strict order and exactly-once processing, use S Q S Fifo. To push one message to many subscribers, including email and S M S, use S N S. For durable copies for each consumer, use S N S plus S Q S. To route events from services and software-as-a-service, or to run schedules, use EventBridge. And to migrate a J M S or A M Q P broker, use Amazon M Q. Exam tip: match the verb: buffer, push, route or migrate.

2.title: AWS Step Functions Workflows
2.text: A W S Step Functions orchestrates workflows as state machines, with Task, Choice, Parallel, Map and Wait states. Retry and Catch handle errors, callbacks can wait for a human, and it calls over two hundred services directly. There are two workflow types. Standard workflows run for up to one year, execute each step exactly once, and suit long-running, auditable workflows. Express workflows run for up to five minutes, execute at least once, handle up to one hundred thousand executions per second, and suit high-volume streaming and Internet of Things work. Exam tip: multi-step logic with retries and branches belongs in Step Functions, not in code inside a Lambda function.

2.title: AWS Lambda and Serverless Patterns
2.text: A W S Lambda runs code without servers. It scales automatically, and you pay for use. Events from S three, S Q S, S N S, EventBridge, A P I Gateway and DynamoDB start functions. The limits to know: fifteen minutes per invocation; memory from one hundred twenty-eight to ten thousand two hundred forty megabytes, with C P U in proportion; and six megabytes for a synchronous request or response. The default is one thousand concurrent executions per Region, and new accounts start lower. Lambda is stateless, so keep data elsewhere. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, the documentation also lists newer options such as Lambda Managed Instances and durable functions. Exam tip: short, event-driven, spiky work is Lambda; over fifteen minutes needs another option.

2.title: Containers: ECS, EKS and Fargate
2.text: Three services come up for containers. Amazon E C S is the A W S-native container orchestrator, with tasks and services; choose it for the simplest A W S-native option. Amazon E K S is managed Kubernetes, Kubernetes-conformant; choose it when you need Kubernetes compatibility or portability. A W S Fargate is serverless compute for E C S and E K S, with no servers to manage. To move an application into containers, package it and its dependencies in an image, store the image in E C R, and run it on E C S or E K S. To run containers on your own servers, there are E C S Anywhere, E K S Anywhere and E K S Distro, the open-source Kubernetes build. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, E C S also lists Managed Instances, and E K S has Auto Mode. Exam tip: containers without managing servers is Fargate; Kubernetes required is E K S.

2.title: Amazon API Gateway
2.text: Amazon A P I Gateway is the front door for Rest, H T T P and WebSocket A P I s, in front of Lambda, E C two, or any H T T P backend. It handles traffic management, throttling, authorization and monitoring. Authorizers can use I A M, Lambda authorizers, or Cognito user pools. Rest A P I s add caching, usage plans and A P I keys, while H T T P A P I s are simpler and cheaper. You also get canary releases, custom domains, W A F and X-Ray support, and edge-optimized, Regional or private endpoints. Exam tip: a managed A P I with throttling, keys and a Lambda backend is A P I Gateway.

2.title: Purpose-Built Managed Services
2.text: Several purpose-built services reduce operational work. Elastic Beanstalk takes your uploaded code and provisions instances, load balancing, scaling and monitoring, at no extra charge. A W S Amplify builds and hosts full-stack web and mobile apps, with Git-based deployment. A W S Device Farm tests web and mobile apps on real devices. The Serverless Application Repository finds, deploys and publishes serverless apps from S A M templates. And A W S Transfer Family gives managed S F T P, F T P S and F T P into S three or E F S; module eleven covers it. And Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets such as database passwords; module two covers it. Exam tip: least operational overhead usually means a purpose-built managed service.

3.title: An Event-Driven Microservice Pattern
3.text: Here is a pattern that ties it together. A P I Gateway receives the request, and a function accepts the order and publishes an event. Queues buffer the work for payment, inventory and email workers. Dead-letter queues catch failures, and retries are safe if workers are idempotent, which means repeating a message has no extra effect. Each microservice owns its data and scales alone. The figure also shows an S three upload that triggers a thumbnail function. Exam tip: accept fast, process later: acknowledge the request, then do the work through queues.

3.title: Lambda, Fargate or EC2?
3.text: Here is the compute decision. Lambda's unit is a function, it runs for up to fifteen minutes, you manage only code, and it is best for event-driven, spiky, short work. Fargate's unit is a container, it has no fixed time limit, you manage the container, and it is best for long-running services and batch jobs. E C two's unit is a virtual server, it has no fixed time limit, you manage the operating system and scaling, and it is best for full control, special hardware or licenses. Exam tip: longer than fifteen minutes, or already a container, points to Fargate; least management for short events is Lambda.

3.title: What the Exam Asks: Scalable and Loosely Coupled
3.text: Here is what the exam asks. Which coupling service: S Q S, S N S, EventBridge, Amazon M Q or Step Functions. Which scaling approach: vertical or horizontal, stateless or stateful. Which load balancer or cache: A L B, N L B, Gateway Load Balancer, ElastiCache or a replica. Which compute: Lambda, Fargate, E C S, E K S or E C two. And which managed service: A P I Gateway, Beanstalk, Amplify or Transfer Family. Exam tip: underline the requirement: least overhead, buffering, fan-out, order or portability.

3.title: Design Check: Lantern and Loom Meets the Holiday Rush
3.text: Here is the Design Check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Checkout waits on the email service: an S Q S queue and a worker. Sessions vanish when a server is replaced: a stateless web tier, with sessions in ElastiCache. Slash A P I and slash images served by different services: one A L B, path rules, and two target groups. Partners need fixed I P addresses on T C P: a Network Load Balancer with Elastic I P addresses. Catalog reads overload the database: read replicas and a cache. One order must reach three consumers: an S N S topic fanning out to S Q S queues. A multi-step order flow with retries: Step Functions. And a public A P I with throttling and keys: A P I Gateway.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Here is the recap. For loose coupling, put queues, topics, event buses and workflows between components. For scaling, scale out, keep tiers stateless, and use caches and read replicas. For entry points, use A L B for H T T P routing, N L B for static I P s and T C P or U D P, and A P I Gateway for A P I s. For messaging, S Q S buffers, S N S fans out, EventBridge routes, Amazon M Q migrates, and Step Functions orchestrates. For compute, Lambda handles short events, Fargate runs containers, and managed services give the least overhead.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. At Lantern and Loom, the checkout service calls the email service directly, and a slow email service delays every order. Which change makes the two components loosely coupled? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: send an email request to an Amazon S Q S queue that a worker reads. Checkout finishes immediately, the worker sends emails at its own pace, and the queue buffers spikes.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. Lantern and Loom's web servers keep shopping-cart sessions in memory, so replacing a server logs customers out. The team wants to scale out freely. What should the architect do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: store sessions in Amazon ElastiCache, so any instance can serve any request. That makes the web tier stateless. Sticky sessions and local disks still tie a customer to one server.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A partner needs to connect to Lantern and Loom over T C P from fixed I P addresses, with very high throughput and low latency. Which load balancer fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic I P address per zone. It works at layer four with very high throughput. An Application Load Balancer works at layer seven, and a Gateway Load Balancer fronts appliances.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. Select two. The product catalog of Lantern and Loom runs on Amazon R D S, and its read traffic is overloading the primary instance. Which two actions reduce the read load? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Read replicas serve read-only copies, and an ElastiCache cache answers repeated reads without reaching the database. A Multi-A Z standby cannot serve reads, and changing backups or standby replication does not reduce read load.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. Lantern and Loom wants a managed, public Rest A P I for its mobile app, with throttling, A P I keys per partner and a Lambda function behind it. Which service should the architect choose? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Amazon A P I Gateway Rest A P I with usage plans. It provides throttling, usage plans and A P I keys, and integrates directly with Lambda.

3.title: Practice Question 6
3.text: Question six. Select two. Which two statements about Amazon S Q S queue types are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Standard queues deliver each message at least once, so consumers should tolerate duplicates. Fifo queues provide ordering and exactly-once processing. Publishing one message to many subscribers is S N S, and a consumer must delete a message after processing it.

3.title: Practice Question 7
3.text: Question seven. When an order is placed, Lantern and Loom must notify the inventory, email and analytics systems. Each system must process messages at its own pace, and a new system must be addable without changing the order service. Which design fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: publish to an S N S topic that has one S Q S queue per system. Fan-out gives each system its own durable buffer, while a single shared queue gives each message to only one consumer.

3.title: Practice Question 8
3.text: Question eight. Lantern and Loom's refund process has several steps, needs retries, branches on the order value, and must wait for a human approval that can take days. Which service should orchestrate it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: a Step Functions Standard workflow with a callback. Standard workflows run for up to a year. A Lambda function is limited to fifteen minutes, and queues and topics do not orchestrate steps.

3.title: Practice Question 9
3.text: Question nine. A nightly job at Lantern and Loom processes catalog images for about forty minutes inside a custom container. The team wants no servers to manage. Which option fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: an A W S Fargate task that runs the container. Fargate runs containers without servers and has no fixed time limit. A Lambda invocation stops after fifteen minutes.

3.title: Practice Question 10
3.text: Question ten. A company is moving an on-premises application that uses J M S to talk to its message broker. It wants to keep the messaging code unchanged. Which service should it choose? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Amazon M Q. It is a managed broker for ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ that supports J M S and other standard protocols, so the code can move without a rewrite.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: A. Question four: A and D. Question five: C. Question six: B and E. Question seven: B. Question eight: D. Question nine: A. Question ten: C. In Module five, we design for high availability and fault tolerance, including disaster recovery.
